extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: A dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It consists of narrative passages from unpublished novels where human subjects are able to guess the last word given the whole passage, but not given only the target sentence preceding the word.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
extraction.citeAs: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, and Raquel Fernández. 2016. The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. arXiv:1606.06031 [cs.CL]
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Passages consisting of a context (averaging 4.6 sentences, at least 50 tokens) and a target sentence were extracted from the Book Corpus. Candidate passages were first automatically filtered by four language models to discard easily predictable target words. A random sample of remaining passages was then tested on human subjects via CrowdFlower to verify that the target word can be guessed from the full passage but cannot be guessed from the target sentence alone.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015), consisting of unpublished novels.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The Book Corpus underwent duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material using a stop word list, resulting in 5,325 novels. The novels were randomly partitioned into disjoint training (2,662 novels) and development+testing sets. Passages where any of four language models assigned the target word a probability >= 0.00175 were excluded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdsourced human evaluation was conducted in three sequential steps: Step 1: one subject guessed the target word based on the full passage; if correct, Step 2: a second subject guessed the word based on the full passage; if also correct, Step 3: subjects were given the target sentence only and allowed up to 3 guesses each, until guessed or reaching 10 unsuccessful guesses. Passages where no subject guessed the word in Step 3 were added to LAMBADA. A strict exact-match requirement was enforced.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Only items with strict hit-or-miss exact agreement were kept (2 out of 2 broad-context guesses correct, 0 out of 10 sentence-only subjects guessing correctly). In the pipeline, 84–86% of items were discarded at Step 1, 6–7% at Step 2, and 3–5% at Step 3, with only about 1 in 25 candidate passages passing all selection criteria.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Up to 12 human subjects per item (2 subjects for full passage, up to 10 subjects for sentence-only condition).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A pre-trained recurrent neural network (Mikolov et al., 2011), and a standard 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward model trained on the Book Corpus.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set and training corpus were made available at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/, with the test set planned to be released at the time of a public competition.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: More than 80% of LAMBADA passages feature the target word or its lemma in the context. Proper nouns are heavily over-represented (48%), followed by common nouns (37%), whereas verbs, adjectives, and adverbs are under-represented. Quoted direct speech is also present significantly more often in LAMBADA passages (71%) than in the input sample (61%).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Standard language models fail by design due to filtering out passages guessable by local context. The strict hit-or-miss matching criterion discards plausible synonyms or paraphrases. The dataset skews heavily toward noun referential expressions and coreference phenomena rather than event tracking or broad-context verb/adverb prediction.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking and evaluating computational models for natural language understanding and broad discourse context tracking; fine-tuning models on development passages.
